(1)
INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are political scientists 2 who specialize in the
analysis of voting, electoral participation, voter
registration and the use of voter registration lists and
other databases to evaluate the effectiveness and
efficiency of the management of voter registration
systems by state and loc al election officials. Their work
includes evaluating the various methods and data sources
used by election officials to maintain and upgrade voter
registration rolls. Amici have served as expert witnesses
and consultants in cases related to purges, mainte nance
of voter registration rolls, and changes to voter
registration procedures. They have also published many
peer-reviewed articles on the subject.
As this case involves the use of various large
government databases for the purpose of identifying
individuals who may be ineligible to register to vote, Amici
seek to assist the court in understanding the inherent
limitations in and potential errors associated with the use
of these databases for the purpose of identifying
noncitizens in state voter registration lists. Amici have
significant academic and practical experience in
evaluating voter registration data, working with local
election officials responsible for the maintenance of voter

Amicus Daniel A Smith is Professor (and former
Chair) of the Department of Political Science at the
University of Florida and a University of Florida
Research Foundation Professor. He has published
numerous articles, book chapters, and reports on politics
in the United States in many of the leading political
science outlets, including the American Political Science
Review, the American Journal of Political Science, and the
Journal of Politics. The past president of the State Politics
and Policy Section of t he American Political Science
Association, Professor Smith’s scholarly research has
examined the effects electoral laws on voting and political
participation in the United States.
Amicus Kenneth R. Mayer is an Emeritus Professor
of American Politics at the University of Wisconsin -
Madison. Dr. Mayer has published numerous books and
scholarly articles on elections and election administration,
including work published in the American J ournal of
Political Science, the Journal of Politics, Legislative
Studies Quarterly, Public Administration Review,
Election Law Journal, PS: Political Science and Politics,
and Regulation. Professor Mayer’s scholarly research are
in American government and  institution, campaign
finance, and election administration.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The core of the legislation challenged in this
litigation, Arizona H.B. 2492 and H.B. 2243 (“the
Challenged Legislation”), is a requirement that county
election officials to cancel the voter registration of any
voter whose citizenship cannot be confirmed a fter
checking certain statutorily specified databases
maintained by municipalities, the State of Arizona, and

3

the federal government. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16 -165(A)(10),
(G)-(K). The statute requires monthly reviews of
registration lists against these databases, and the
subsequent removal of registered voters, including within
90 days of elections.
The citizenship check mechanism is premised on two
assumptions: (i) that the databases to be consulted are
reliable sources to determine citizenship information and
(ii) that there is a reliable process by which data can be
matched to voter registration re cords. Both of these
assumptions are wrong.
First, as confirmed by Amici’s decades of experience
working with and analyzing voter records and public
databases, and reviewing prior attempts by state officials
to use these databases to confirm citizenship, the quality
of information in these databases  cannot provide a basis
for confidently verifying the citizenship of particular
people. By and large, these databases were not designed
to verify citizenship, and for a myriad of reasons, they are
incapable of doing so without significant error rates.
Second, the results of the matching processes which
have been employed to compare voter records with other
databases have proven repeatedly to be massively
inaccurate. Amici’s research and investigations
demonstrate that matching data across databases with
different architectures and without common fields poses
inherent difficulties that inevitably introduce a second
source of error.
Errors in this context —particularly the false
identification of an eligible voter as ineligible because of
misidentification as a noncitizen —have serious
consequences. When a voter is denied access to the polls
based on such false identification in the day s and weeks
leading up to an election, as a practical matter, there may
be no time to remedy an erroneous removal.

4

ARGUMENT
One of the key mechanisms of the Challenged
Legislation is the requirement for county election officials
to remove voters whose citizenship cannot be
independently verified by matching their voter
information against information contained in a discrete
set of specified databases. The Arizona legislature’s
confidence in this process, as well as in the underlying
technology, was unwarranted. And if the Challenged
Legislation is allowed to take effect, it will almost
certainly result in efforts to remove prope rly registered
voters due to common and well -known limitations of the
underlying data and the flawed process of matching data
across databases.
I. VOTER RECORD “MATCHING” HAS MANY WELL -
KNOWN FLAWS
Based on Amici’s long experience with the relevant
databases, citizenship verification procedures that rely on
matching records across large databases have many
flaws. For purposes of this analysis, these flaws fall into
two broad categories: the quality of the information in the
underlying databases, and errors in the process of
matching records across databases.
A. The Data Quality of the Designated Databases Is
Inadequate to Accurately Verify Citizenship
The Challenged Legislation requires county election
officials to check citizenship against four identified
databases – (i) the “driver license database maintained by
the [Arizona] department of transportation,” (ii) “the
social security administration data base,” (iii) “the
systematic alien verification for entitlements program
maintained by” the United States Citizenship and
Immigration Services, and (iv) the “electronic verification
of vital events system maintained by” the National
Association for Public Health Statistics and Information

5

Systems”—as well as unspecified “relevant city, town,
county, state, and federal databases. . . .” Ariz. Rev. Stat.
§ 16 -165(G)-(K) (collectively, the “Designated
Databases”). The data in each of these databases are
inadequate to reliably verify citizenship, for at least one of
three key reasons: (i) the lack of comprehensiveness of the
data, including the lack of consistency in data maintained,
(ii) the staleness of the data, and (iii) mundane data entry
errors.
1. The Databases Lack the Comprehensiveness
and Consistency to Accurately Confirm
Citizenship
The ability of a database to accurately confirm
citizenship is necessarily limited by the scope of the data
in the database and whether the data has consistently
tracked citizenship. As the National Research Council
summarized in its 2010 report Improving State Voter
Registration Databases  “completeness refers to the
presence in the database of all individuals who should be
in the database.”3
None of the Designated Databases has as its primary
purpose the tracking of citizenship data. The Arizona
Department of Transportation (ADOT) database’s
purpose is to allow status of drivers’ licensure to be
tracked, while both the Social Security Administration
(SSA) databases and the U.S. Citizenship and
Immigration Services (US CIS) Systematic Alien
Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system are
designed to track entitlement or eligibility to benefits.
Not surprisingly, therefore, they are all inadequate,
separately or in combination, to provide citizenship
verification.

3 Nat’l Acads. of Scis., Eng’g, & Med. , Improving State Voter
Registration Databases  (2010) at 17,
https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/12788/

6

Indeed, all of the Designated Databases have
significant gaps in their coverage, particularly gaps in
tracking citizenship status.
For example, the Social Security Administration did
not start collecting evidence of citizenship until 1973 and
did not begin consistently maintaining citizenship
information until 1981. See Soc. Sec. Admin., Social
Security Number Chronology,
https://www.ssa.gov/history/ssn/ssnchron.html; Letter
from Social Security Administration to Fair Elections
Center (Jul. 13, 2023) (“SSA/FEC Letter”),
https://perma.cc/KS2N-U2US. Merely having a social
security number is not an indication that an individual is
a U.S. citizen, as noncitizens are permitted to obtain social
security numbers for tax and benefits purposes. Soc. Sec.
Admin., Foreign Workers and Social Security Numbers ,
https://www.ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10107.pdf. The SSA
warns that SSA data used for any purpose other than a
SSA program purpose “may not be current.” SSA/FEC
Letter at 2. In 2023, SSA estimated that approximately
one-fourth of its records lacked an indication of
citizenship. Id. at 3.
The SAVE system is a system of information created
in 1986 to verify whether noncitizens are eligible for
certain government benefits. See Pub. L. No. 99-603, title
I, §§ 121(a)(1)(C), 121(c)(1). As such, the system was not
designed or intended to identify  U.S. citizens. Privacy
Impact Assessment for the Systematic Alien Verification
Entitlements Program, DHS Ref. N. DHS/USCIS/PIA -
006(c), Dept. Of Homeland Sec., 2 -3 (June 30, 2020),
privacy-pia-uscis006c-save-july2020.pdf. SAVE does not
track citizenship status of native-born U.S. citizens and in
some cases does not track citizenship information for
individuals with derived citizenship. App. 204a.
As for the Arizona Department of Transportation,
like Motor Vehicle Departments across the country, it

7

only has records for individuals with a driver’s license or
who have obtained some other form of state -issued
identification. Public opinion surveys estimate that
approximately 21 million voting-aged U.S. citizens did not
have non-expired driver’s licenses. See Univ. of Md. Ctr.
for Democracy & Civ. Engagement, Who Lacks ID in
America Today? An Exploration of Voter ID Access,
Barriers, and Knowledge  (Jan. 2024),
https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter
%20ID%202023%20survey%20Key%20Results%20Jan%
202024%20%281%29.pdf. In this respect, ADOT is typical
of state Motor Vehicle Departments across the country.
But ADOT is atypical for two reasons. First, ADOT
started collecting data for lawful presence status in 1996
pursuant to Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 41-1080, ten to thirty years
earlier than most other states. 4 Second, Arizona is one of
the few states that effectively allow permanent licenses
that do not need to be renewed; in Arizona, drivers’
licenses are valid until the recipient turns 65. Ariz. Rev.
Stat. § 28 -3171. See generally Ams. for Older Driver
Safety, All State by State , https://afods.org/states/state-

4 In most other states, Motor Vehicle Departments did not start to
collect lawful presence status data until the implementation of the
2005 REAL ID Act, which is still being fully implemented by states
following its effective date in 2025. See, e.g., K. Van Cleve, Real ID
deadline is weeks away and most states aren’t fully compliant yet ,
CBS News (Apr. 22, 2025) (reporting 17 states were less than 50%
compliant, and 30 - states were less than 70% compliant),
https://www.cbsnews.com/news/real -id-deadline-weeks-away-moststates-not-fully-compliant-yet/; A. Kimmery, Twenty years later the
REAL ID debate refuses to go away , Biometric Update (Apr. 29,
2025) (reporting only 60 percent of driver’s licenses and
identification cards were REAL ID
compliant),https://www.biometricupdate.com/202504/twenty -yearslater-the-real-id-debate-refuses-to-go-away. This means that
individuals who obtained or renewed their license prior to
implementation in their state could do so without being asked to
present proof of citizenship status .

8

by-state-all/. The significance of this is that the ADOT
database does not have citizenship information for most
individuals who first obtained a driver’s license before
1996 who have not yet turned 65.
2. The Timing of Data Updates and the Staleness
of Data Affect the Accuracy of Citizenship
Information
In Amici’s experience, administrative records
maintained by federal, state, and local governments
typically are not updated continuously, and thus are often
out of date and reflect a person’s status as of some earlier
date and so misrepresent their current  status. See
generally R. Wang & D. Strong, Beyond Accuracy: What
Data Quality Means to Data Consumers , 12 J. of Mgmt.
Info. Sys. 5-33 (1996).
The risks of relying on such databases for verifying
that voters are citizens are exemplified by how databases
treat citizenship. To be clear, Amici are unaware of any
centralized, continuously updated database of citizenship
status in the United States. Rather, a person’s citizenship
may be recorded late, or not at all, in any given database.
The same observation holds true when an individual has a
change in status, such as when they naturalize; that fact
may never be recorded in the relevant databases, or there
may be a time lag before it is entered. In other words,
whether the database is updated and the timing of that
update affect the accuracy of the database’s citizenship
information.
Each of the Designated Databases poses this risk of
providing inaccurate citizenship information. With regard
to the Social Security Administration, the agency
represented that the citizenship information in its
databases “merely represents a snapshot of t he
individual’s citizenship status at the time of their
interaction with SSA.” SSA/FEC Letter at 2. This has
been repeatedly confirmed. For example, a 2018 U.S.

9

Census Bureau report comparing Census survey
responses with SSA records found widespread
inconsistencies between census responses and
administrative records regarding citizenship. J. D. Brown
et al., Understanding the quality of alternative
citizenship data sources for the 2020 census . US Census
Bureau, Ctr. for Econ. Stud. (Wash., D.C. 2018 (revised
2019)), https://www2.census.gov/ces/wp/2018/CES -WP-
18-38R.pdf. Although the report notes that some of this
discrepancy may be the result of noncitizen respondents
misreporting their status , the report also found that
administrative records may fail to capture naturalizations
or record them only after a delay.
With regard to SAVE, evidence was presented at
trial below about lags and other timing issues in how
promptly USCIS updates changes to records, including
name changes and changes in citizenship status. Because
the information in SAVE is provided by multiple agencies,
it is particularly vulnerable to internal inconsistencies and
lags in the information it is collecting. USCIS personnel
testified in the proceeding below that it may take “days”
to address discrepancies in data, and that updates to key
information (like name changes) depend on self-reporting.
Rule 30(b)(6) Deposition of USCIS  at 2206, Mi Familia
Vota et al v. Fontes et al , No. 22-cv-00509-SRB (D. Ariz.
Oct. 16, 2023), ECF No. 571 -6. These and other factors
undermine SAVE’s reliability for purposes of
determining citizenship. While SAVE may be able to note
whether an individual has an Alien Registration Number
(“A-Number”), academic reviews have established that
hundreds of thousands o f people who are recorded in
SAVE as having A -Numbers have since become U.S.
citizens. See generally R. Li et al.. Why Do Immigrants
Participate in Politics Less Than Native-Born Citizens?
A Formative Years Explanation, 5 J. of Race, Ethnicity
& Politics, 62-91 (Mar. 2020); L. Bass et al, Impacting the

10

Political Landscape: Who Registers and Votes Among
Naturalized Americans, 23 Pol. Behav., 103-130 (2001).
Nationally, databases maintained by state
Departments of Motor Vehicles reflect a person’s
citizenship status only at a single point in time—when that
person last interacted with the agency —typically in
obtaining or renewing a driver’s license or other
identification. State Departments of Motor Vehicles rely
on individuals to affirmatively provide updates to their
citizenship status. There is no legal requirement that
people update their status when their citizenship changes,
such as when they naturalize. M ost people do not have a
clear need to update their status before their credentials
expire. And updating citizenship status typically incurs a
cost, including an in -person visit to the Department of
Motor Vehicles.
The ADOT database exemplifies these
insufficiencies. Evidence presented below confirmed that
ADOT database information on citizenship or authorized
presence for noncitizens reflects a person’s status only at
the time they obtain their driver’s license, and is typically
updated only when the individual has to renew or update
their license. As noted above, in Arizona, renewals are
much less frequent than in most other states; most
Arizona driver’s licenses do not expire until someone
turns 65, while licenses for legal permanent residents are
valid as long as their permanent resident card is valid–up
to ten years. The consequence is that information about
someone’s citizenship in the ADOT database is often stale
and inaccurate.
Even when a naturalized citizen updates their
citizenship status with ADOT or other database
proprietors, bureaucratic gears may grind slowly as the
new information makes its way through various
databases. And it is common for there to be a lag between
a particular database’s information about an individual’s

11

citizenship status and a new citizen’s date of
naturalization.
3. Data Entry Errors Undermine the Reliability of
Citizenship Information in the Designated
Databases
Amici’s own research and academic literature
confirm that large administrative databases maintained
by local, state, and federal agencies contain numerous
clerical errors. See generally D. Hand, Statistical
Challenges of Administrative and Transactional Data ,
181 J. of the Royal Stat. Soc’y 555 -605 (2018); J. Groen,
Sources of Error in Survey and Administrative Data:
The Importance of Reporting Procedures , 28 J. of Off.
Stats. 173-198 (2012). Clerical errors and inconsistencies
may arise for multiple reasons, such as registrants mis -
entering information on forms, clerks mis -transcribing
information into the database, clerks incorrectly
transcribing handwri ting, transposing letters and
numbers, inconsistently treating special characters such
as spaces and hyphens, and misspelling name variants,
among other errors. For example, in its 2010 report, the
National Research Council identified other potential
sources of error:
One common source of error in the data is data
entry. Applicants typically submit handwritten
voter registration forms that are sent to the
election official. The applicant can make a
mistake, forget to answer a question, or not write
legibly. The form or its information could be
altered in transmission (a field could get
smudged or torn or otherwise damaged in postal

12

handling, for example). Keying errors result in
mistranscriptions.5
The challenge of data entry errors due to mis -
transcribing names is particularly significant for
individuals with uncommon names that may be unfamiliar
to state or federal agency clerks, such as those born in
another country or the children of recent immigrants.
The quality of data entry also depends on how central
a field is to the work of the agency that collects it.
Administrative data are a by-product of operational tasks,
and an agency has little reason to verify or update
information that is peripheral to th ose tasks. See
generally Hand., supra; Groen, supra. Each such
peripheral field is therefore more prone to errors,
including missing values.
Like the information in all massive databases, SSA
records suffer from data entry errors. A 2012 Inspector
General report to the U.S. Congress characterized the
SSA database as “generally accurate,” but noted that
there were errors or variances in 6 percent of the records
sampled when compared to Department of Homeland
Security (DHS) records. Off. of Inspector Gen., Soc. Sec.
Admin.. Accuracy of the Social Security
Administration’s NUMIDENT . Report: A -08-12-11280
(2012) , https://oig-files.ssa.gov/audits/full/A-08-12-
11280.pdf. Other SSA Inspector General reports have
noted the use of nicknames and insertion of spaces and
hyphens prevent the utility of the data to verify voting
eligibility. See Off. of Inspector Gen., Soc. Sec. Admin., A-
03-09-29115, Accuracy of the Help America Vote
Verification Program Responses  7-8 (2009)  ,
https://oig.ssa.gov/~assets/audits/full/a-03-09-29115.pdf.

5 Nat’l Acads. of Scis., Eng’g, & Med., Improving State Voter
Registration Databases: Final Report  17 (2010),
https://doi.org/10.17226/12788 .

13

The SAVE system suffers from these same issues.
Shannon Slattery, Acting Chief of the SAVE Program at
USCIS, testified in the proceeding below that:
Principally, data integrity issues stem largely
from the way data is entered into a system.
Oftentimes we find users transpose data;
numbers and letters may be out of sequence.
There are a lot of typographical errors.
Rule 30(b)(6) Deposition of USCIS at 2279,  Mi Familia
Vota et al v. Fontes et al , No. 22-cv-00509-SRB (D. Ariz.
Oct. 16, 2023), ECF No. 571-6.
Mariah Doolittle, SAVE’s Chief of Product
Management and Delivery further testified that:
[S]ome of the data errors for name discrepancies
could be that the name is too long; the string of
characters could be too long for the system.
Because of that, with older system records, it
could have been truncated, or if there was a
hyphenated name, that would have caused issues
in the past.
Id. at 2281. According to this testimony, whether the
SAVE system can handle compound, unhyphenated last
names “is very dependent on [the] source systems.” Id. at
2282.
Similarly, the ADOT database, like all massive
databases with millions of records, has simple data entry
errors. As the Arizona’s Director of the Motor Vehicle
Division Eric Jorgenson testified at trial, ADOT’s weekly
checks find that its records have an e rror rate of
“approximately 10 to 15%.” App. 203a.
As discussed in more detail below, each of these
errors and inconsistencies can cause election officials to
fail to match a voter registration record with the proper
record in an external database. The information sought by
such matching may be incorrect, leading election officials

14

to incorrectly identify an applicant’s citizenship status,
possibly triggering the denial of voting rights.
B. Matching Processes Have Inherent Limitations
That Generally Make Them Unsuitable to Verify
Citizenship
Separate and apart from limitations and accuracy of
the data in the databases it relies on for citizenship
verification, the Challenged Legislation presents a second
source of errors because it is dependent on the process of
matching records across databases. Matching is the
“procedure by which attributes of one data registration
record are compared to attributes of another record (for
example, a new voter registration application, a DMV
driver’s license, an SSA record, a reco rd in a database of
felons, and so on).”6
Matching errors arise when databases share no
unique identifier that can link records belonging to the
same person. When there is no such identifier, matching
must then rely on less reliable information, such as names,
dates of birth, addresses, the last f our digits of a social
security number, or a state driver’s license number.
While record linkage without a unique identifier is
common in public health and medicine, social service
administration, and economics, it is not infallible. Rather,
matching is vulnerable both because of inaccuracies in the
underlying data and because the  available identifying
information may be limited, inaccurate, or unstable. Such
matches can err in two directions: records belonging to
different people may be treated as the same person (a
false match), and records belonging to the same person
may fail to link (a missed match). See generally I. Fellegi
& A. Sunter, A Theory for Record Linkage , 64 J. of the

6 Nat’l Acads. of Scis., Eng’g, & Med., Improving State Voter
Registration Databases: Final Report  19-20 (2010),
https://doi.org/10.17226/12788 .

15

Am. Stat. Ass’n 1183-1210 (1969); J. Doidge & K. Harron,
Reflections on Modern Methods: Linkage Error Bias, 48
Int’l J. of Epidemiology 2050-60 (2019).
Vulnerabilities also arise from the matching protocol
used. Matching methodologies are sometimes referred to
as “hard” or “exact” matches or “soft” or “probabilistic”
matches. “Hard” matches rely on an identical unique
identifier in both databases, such as  a driver’s license or
social security number. “Soft” or “probabilistic” matches
seek to determine whether there is a match or near match
in other data fields, such as name or birth date, and are
usually expressed as a probability. Both “hard” and “soft”
matching methodologies create risk of error. Because a
“hard” match depends on the  presence of a unique
identifier, it may have “missed matches” and be
underinclusive in failing to identify actual matches if, for
example, one of the two databases being matched has
incomplete or inaccurately entered identifiers.
Conversely, a “soft” matc h may be overinclusive and
identify false matches based on partial data. For example,
a database search by last name and birth date is
unreliable when there are millions of records to search.
The number of individuals that share the same last name
and birt h date is surprisingly large. See, e.g., M.
McDonald & J. Levitt, Seeing Double Voting: An
Extension of the Birthday Problem , 7 Election Law J.
111-122 (2008).
Under the Challenged Legislation, matching is
supposed to occur between registered voter databases
and databases maintained by other agencies (the DHS,
the SSA, ADOT) whose purpose is not to track voter
eligibility or citizenship, and whose data quality is sues
(discussed supra in Argument I.A) pose significant
challenges to determining accurately whether a
registered voter is a citizen.

16

The risks of inaccurate assessment of voter eligibility
are magnified here because  these databases are to be
matched  against voter registration files. Like all large
administrative databases maintained by governmental
entities, voter registration files a re known to contain
errors and inconsistencies in how voters’ information is
recorded and maintained, which makes matching them
against other administrative databases particularly
perilous. See generally M. McDonald, The True
Electorate: A Cross -Validation of Voter Registration
Files and Election Survey Demographics, 71 Pub. Op. Q.
588-602 (2007); E. Shino et al., Verifying Voter
Registration Records, 48 Am. Pol. Rsch. (2020); C. Cooper
& J. Blitzer, The Curious Case of the Missing Data:
Registration Roll-Off and Election Administration,  4 J.
of Election Admin., Rsch. & Prac. 91-101 (2025). Agencies
use different conventions to record the same information,
including name order, compound or hyphenated
surnames, transliteration, and date and address formats.
Unless these are standardized before linkage, records for
the same person may fail to match, and records for
different people may match in error. P. Christen, Data
Matching (Springer 2012); L. Zhang, Topics of statistical
theory for register-based statistics and data integration ,
66 Statistica Neerlandica 41-63 (2012).
Scholars have long found that efforts to match voter
registration records against other large databases are
particularly challenging—at best imperfect and at worst
severely flawed. G. Stuart, Databases, felons, and voting:
Bias and partisanship of the Florida felons list in the
2000 elections, 119 Pol. Sci. Q. 453-475 (2004); L. Minnite,
The Myth of Voter Fraud  (Cornell Univ. Press 2010); R.
Hasen, The Voting Wars: From Florida 2000 to the Next
Election Meltdown (Yale Univ. Press 2012); R. Scher, The
Politics of Disenfranchisement: Why is it So Hard to Vote
in America? (Routledge 2015); T. Wang, The Politics of

17

Voter Suppression: Defending and Expanding
Americans’ Right to Vote  (Cornell Univ. Press 2012); D.
Biggers & D.A. Smith, Does Threatening Their
Franchise Make Registered Voters More Likely to
Participate? Evidence From an Aborted Voter Purge, 50
Brit. J. of Pol. Sci. 933 -954 (2020); G. Huber, et al., The
Racial Burden of Voter List Maintenance Errors:
Evidence from Wisconsin’s Supplemental Movers Poll
Books, 7 Sci. Advances, eabe4498 (2021). As the National
Research Council summarized in 2010:
Because of data quality issues and the lack of a
universally used unique identifier, record
matching cannot be done perfectly in this
context, that is, with zero false positives and zero
false negatives. The consequence is that
achieving the goal of a simultaneously 100
percent accurate and 100 percent complete voter
registration list is virtually impossible. . . . From
a technical standpoint, th e hard problem in
matching usually lies not in identifying potential
matches (e.g., pairs of records that may have
some but not all elements in common) but rather
in how to handle the potential matches that are
identified. . . . Determining whether two rec ords
refer to the same individual is usually the
problematic step.7
The experience of jurisdictions trying to use
databases to identify noncitizens on their voter rolls
illustrates this difficulty, as matching technologies have
shown time and time again to identify large numbers of
false positives. For example:

II. USING THE DESIGNATED DATABASES TO
DISQUALIFY VOTERS IS ESPECIALLY UNRELIABLE
IN THE NINETY DAY WINDOW PRIOR TO AN
ELECTION
While errors in efforts to match records to validate
citizenship are both predictable and common, the
consequences of such errors are particularly serious if
they occur in the days and weeks leading up to an election.
As a practical matter, voters may not receive notice
that the validity of their registration has been challenged
in time to challenge an erroneous removal from the voter
rolls. In Arizona, the deadline to register to vote is 29 days
before Election Day, Ar iz. Rev. Stat. § 16 -120(A), and
most other states have a registration deadline of 15 to 30
days before the election. Accordingly, if —as the
Challenged Legislation requires —a county election
official relies on the Designated Databases and
erroneously removes an eligible voter, there is little time
to challenge the incorrect removal. The steps to fix the
problem can be time -consuming: the voter must receive
the notice of their removal, obtain and gather information
and documents to contest the removal, and follow the
administrative procedure to submit the necessary
information; then the county official must review the
information (during the busiest time of their year in the
weeks prior to an election) and make th e necessary
change to the registration rolls, all in sufficient time for
the voter to cast their ballot.
In Amici’s experience, county election officials are not
well equipped to address these tedious, case -by-case
reviews of individual voter eligibility, particularly when
the reviews involve sorting through conflicting
information from diverse databases or w here an
individual voter provides information inconsistent with

21

results from databases upon which the officials are
required by law to rely. This process is likely to be
significantly prone to error, particularly during the
busiest time of the election cycle for election officials in
the weeks leading up to a general election.
CONCLUSION
The judgment of the court of appeals should be
reversed.
